newsitem.title: PERU: Hostages in Peru receive prayers, turkey.
newsitem.headline: Hostages in Peru receive prayers, turkey.

text.p: The 105 hostages held by Marxist guerrillas were given a Christmas feast on Wednesday and prayed for release from the Japanese ambassador's residence, but there was no sign of a break in the armed standoff.

The Christmas dinner, including platters of turkey and fruit, came compliments of Peru's first family and its delivery was supervised by President Alberto Fujimori's daughter, Keiko, who asked the heavily armed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels to "lay down their arms."

Keiko, the 21-year-old first lady of Peru, crossed police lines while inside a bullet-proof Mercedes limousine to a street outside the besieged residence where the hostages began their second week of captivity.
She did not enter the residence, remaining inside the car outside the ambassador's home for about five minutes. Her uncle, the president's brother, is one of the hostages.
Presidential palace chefs who arrived by bus delivered the seasonal feast to Red Cross workers who wheeled the meals on carts up to the front portal of the ambassador's residence.
"Thank-you, brothers. Happy Christmas," the hostages replied minutes later on a sign held up to a window.

Catholic bishop Jose Luis Cipriani entered the building and spent the morning celebrating mass and saying prayers with the captives, who include Japanese businessmen, Latin American ambassadors and high-ranking Peruvian government officials.
Outside in the streets, a choir sang carols to bring Yuletide cheer to the captives. Lima's normal misty gray clouds lifted, giving way to bright sunshine.

Red Cross officials described the captives' health as good and said the delivery of fresh water and new supplies of medicine eased the risk of new cases of diarrhoea and eye infections that struck some hostages last week.
But Red Cross spokesman Roland Bigler had no information to offer about the possibility of more hostage releases.
"We can't say," he told a news conference. "To give a reply would be pure speculation and we don't get involved in speculation of that kind."
One hostage was granted his freedom on Tuesday but as Christmas Day passed there was no sign others would be released on the holiday.
Uruguayan ambassador Tabare Bocalandro did not say why he was released but officials in Montevideo said he was swapped for two MRTA rebels from jail in Uruguay earlier in the day.

Furious at the apparent concession, the Peruvian government pulled out its top diplomat from Uruguay. Local media recalled bitterly that Uruguay signed a declaration by Latin American nations vowing not to give in to terrorist demands.
President Fujimori, who is the son of Japanese immigrants, has flatly rejected all of the demands made by the guerrillas and said they must release the captives and hand over their weapons.

The rebels have vowed not to surrender until their request for the release of more than 400 comrades from Peruvian jails is granted and have demanded a restructuring of the economy to help Peru's impoverished masses.

Japanese media covering the crisis speculated that a behind-the-scenes deal might be worked out under which the MRTA rebels would fly to asylum in Cuba after releasing the hostages but there has been no official word on this.
Japan has around 30 nationals inside the besieged residence, including Tokyo's ambassador Morihisa Aoki, host of the ill-fated cocktail reception Dec. 17 that was stormed by the MRTA rebels.

Always tight-lipped with the press, Fujimori has closeted himself with generals and top advisers and cut himself off from the media during the crisis. Presidential officials have given no information to the hordes of waiting journalists.

Earlier in the day, Russian president Boris Yeltsin called on the Group of Seven leading industrialised nations to consider sending a task force to Peru to help solve the crisis but there was no immediate reaction from Fujimori, who has so far rejected offers of military or police help.
